issues.issue: The start and end dates are handwritten and effectively illegible on the face of the instrument, so the term of the lease/license cannot be fixed from the words used. A court would have to construe what dates the parties actually inserted.

This dated term sits against Lease paragraph 1, which says the term begins on the first day of the month following shipment for the number of months in Block A, and against License Section 5.1, which keys the term to the same Block A. The three cannot be reconciled without construction.

"Includes Protocols as needed for personal injury, or rehab" gives no boundary to which protocols are included or who decides that they are "needed." "1 hour per month of our time ... (You calling us)" is likewise undefined as to carry-over and forfeiture.

The package described here (Loosening and Recovery Protocols plus protocols as needed for injury or rehab) does not match the License Agreement Section 2 grant, which lists only "ARP loosening and recovery," "ARP Therapy Protocol Limited" and "60 Minutes a month specialist support." The scope of what was actually licensed is therefore internally inconsistent.

Nothing on the face of the option shows whether it was elected, and "to set up your plan" gives no measurable content to what the weekly calls must deliver. The word "Yearly" also sits unexplained against the 5-year license.

The weekly calls promised here ("us calling you") run against the base package's "1 hour per month of our time (You calling us)" and against Section 3's support obligation of monthly Minneapolis seminars. Which support regime governs is not resolved.

"IT IS A FDA VIOLATION TO RESELL" is a bare legal assertion with no operative obligation attached, and "THE ARP" is used without definition. Whether this is a covenant, a representation, or mere notice is open.

The Lessee is identified as "ARP Wave Austin, Garrett Salpeter," leaving it ambiguous whether the lessee is the business entity, the individual, or both jointly. That identification drives who is personally bound.

The granting language leases "the equipment, machinery and appurtenances described above," but page 1 describes only license packages, hours and prices — no equipment is in fact described. The subject matter of the lease has to be supplied from outside the words.

The term is measured by "the period of months indicated in Block A on Page 1," but no block on page 1 is labelled "Block A" and page 1 states calendar dates rather than a number of months. The reference cannot be applied as written.

A term beginning "the first day of the month following the date of shipment" conflicts with the page 1 "Lease/License Start Date" and with License Section 5.1, which makes the agreement effective on that stated start date. Two different commencement rules govern the same period.

Rent is "the sum shown in Block B above," but no block on page 1 bears that label, and "paid in advance or before the first day of each month" is garbled (evidently "on or before"). The amount and timing of rent cannot be read off the document.

This clause assumes monthly rental instalments, whereas page 1 states a single discounted lump-sum license price plus shipping with no monthly figure. Whether any monthly rent was ever payable cannot be squared with the front page.

The parties' stipulation that this is a "True Lease" under UCC Article 2A is a label whose accuracy a court would test against the substance of the transaction. The 48-hour inspection deadline itself is definite.

The promise that Lessor "shall repair defects to the equipment free of charge" is hard to reconcile with paragraph 8, which puts the entire risk of loss and damage on Lessee and makes Lessee "liable to repair the equipment at its expense." Who bears repair cost for a non-negligent defect is genuinely uncertain.

The final clause says no defect "SHALL RELIEVE LESSER OF THE OBLIGATION," an evident misspelling of Lessee that leaves the operative subject in doubt. The carve-out "EXCEPT AS IS SPECIFICALLY PROVIDED HEREIN" is also unspecified.

The cap at "the total amount of rent paid" is awkward where page 1 states a lump-sum license price rather than rent, but no other provision squarely contradicts it. Nothing specific in the instrument conflicts.

"Public ability" insurance is a mistyping of public liability insurance, and the required "form and amount" is left to the Lessor's approval without standard. The insurance obligation cannot be measured as written.

Making Lessee "liable to repair the equipment at its expense" for any repairable damage cannot be squared with paragraph 4, which obliges Lessor to repair defects free of charge absent Lessee misuse or negligence. The two allocate the same cost differently.

The default trigger refers to a document "fumished to the Lessee in connection with the transaction" proving false, when the sense plainly requires documents furnished to the Lessor; the parties are reversed. Read literally, Lessee defaults on Lessor's own misstatements.

The cross-default making "any default under the License Agreement or any other agreement signed contemporaneously" a default here sits against paragraph 18, which declares this Lease to be the entire agreement between the parties. Whether other instruments are part of the bargain is left unresolved.

The indemnity covers "any and all claims ... arising out of, connected with, or resulting from the equipment," with an illustrative list introduced by "including without limiting the generality of the foregoing." Whether the general words reach claims caused by the Lessor's own fault is left open.

"Acting outside the scope of use for the equipment" is not defined anywhere, and the duty is imposed on the "Licensee" inside an equipment lease that elsewhere speaks only of the Lessee. The boundary of permitted use is left to argument.

The second sentence authorises Lessor to apply against "amounts owing Lessor hereunder any amounts which might ... be owed to Lessor or any affiliate of Lessor by Lessee," which is circular; a workable set-off requires amounts owed by Lessor to Lessee. The direction of the offset is a drafting error that changes the meaning.

The Lease is declared "the entire agreement between the parties hereto" although the same signed document contains the License Agreement, which paragraph 12 expressly cross-defaults, and which itself contains its own integration clause in Section 7. Which instrument integrates what is genuinely unresolved.

Joint and several liability depends on who is "named in this Lease," and the granting clause names "ARP Wave Austin, Garrett Salpeter" without saying whether that is one lessee or two. The two provisions read together leave personal liability uncertain.

"Venue for the enforcement of this Agreement" does not say whether it captures only contract claims or also related tort, trade secret and statutory claims between the parties. The reach of the clause is the classic point of construction.

The clause speaks of "this Agreement" although it appears in the Lease, which paragraph 18 defines as a separate instrument from the License Agreement that carries its own identical venue clause. Which document's disputes are covered has to be worked out across the two.

This clause permits notice by personal delivery, telegram or first class mail, while License Agreement Section 8 requires notices to be sent by facsimile or overnight courier. Notice given under one instrument may be ineffective under the other.

The preamble leaves the Licensee's name blank — "and ______ ('Licensee')" — so the operative License Agreement never identifies the party to be bound. Who the Licensee is must be supplied from outside the clause.

The blank must be filled from page 1 and Section 8, which name "ARP Wave Austin, Garrett Salpeter," leaving open whether the entity, the individual, or both are the Licensee. That identification cannot be settled within the four corners.
